name: Immunotactoid glomerulopathy
aliases: glomerulonephritis with organised microtubular monoclonal immunoglobulin deposits

reference.source: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology / Brenner and Rector's The Kidney
clinicalPearls: A rare organised deposition glomerulopathy defined by parallel-arrayed microtubular deposits that are Congo-red negative and typically larger and more ordered than fibrillary GN fibrils
Presents with proteinuria, often nephrotic-range, together with microscopic haematuria, hypertension and renal impairment
Deposits are frequently monoclonal (commonly IgG with light-chain restriction), and immunofluorescence should be examined for clonality
Strongly associated with underlying B-cell lymphoproliferative disorders and paraproteinaemia, notably chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma
Electron microscopy is decisive: hollow microtubules arranged in parallel bundles, in contrast to the randomly oriented solid fibrils of fibrillary GN
DNAJB9 is characteristically negative, helping separate it from fibrillary glomerulonephritis
Treatment is directed at any underlying clone (clone-directed therapy for paraprotein-related disease) alongside supportive renal measures
reference.pathophysiology: Immunotactoid glomerulopathy results from glomerular deposition of immunoglobulin that organises into hollow microtubular structures, usually 30 to 50 nanometres in diameter, aligned in parallel arrays within the mesangium and capillary walls. The deposits are commonly monoclonal, reflecting an underlying clonal B-cell or plasma-cell population that produces an immunoglobulin prone to crystalline or microtubular self-assembly. Accumulation disrupts the glomerular filtration barrier and triggers a proliferative or membranoproliferative injury pattern, causing proteinuria, haematuria and progressive glomerulosclerosis. The association with lymphoproliferative disease and paraproteinaemia underpins the rationale for treating the causative clone.
additionalDifferentials: Fibrillary glomerulonephritis (randomly arranged fibrils, DNAJB9 positive)
additionalInvestigations: Renal biopsy with electron microscopy showing parallel microtubular deposits
Immunofluorescence for immunoglobulin subclass and light-chain restriction
DNAJB9 staining to distinguish from fibrillary GN
Serum and urine protein electrophoresis and serum free light chains
Bone marrow examination and flow cytometry when a clone is suspected
Cross-sectional imaging and haematology review for lymphoproliferative disease
redFlags: Newly detected monoclonal protein or lymphoproliferative disorder
Rapidly progressive renal impairment or crescentic change
Systemic features of an underlying haematological malignancy
reference.prognosis: Renal outcome is closely tied to identification and treatment of the underlying clone; clone-directed therapy can stabilise or improve renal function, whereas untreated disease tends to progress. Because of the strong haematological association, prognosis also depends on the behaviour of the associated lymphoproliferative disorder.
pitfalls: Conflating it with fibrillary glomerulonephritis without electron microscopy and DNAJB9 testing
Failing to search for an underlying lymphoproliferative disorder once monoclonality is found
Treating with generic immunosuppression rather than clone-directed therapy
Overlooking the diagnosis because of its rarity in a nephrotic patient
management: Treatment directed at the underlying B-cell or plasma-cell clone, such as rituximab-based regimens for chronic lymphocytic leukaemia or lymphoplasmacytic disease and bortezomib-based therapy for plasma-cell clones
Renin-angiotensin system blockade with an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker to reduce proteinuria, alongside blood pressure control
Supportive management of nephrotic syndrome, including diuretics for oedema, lipid-lowering therapy and attention to thromboembolic risk
Monitoring of renal function, proteinuria and the paraprotein or serum free light chains to assess response
Renal replacement therapy or transplantation for progressive kidney failure, with awareness of the risk of disease recurrence in the graft
Joint management by nephrology and haematology with bone marrow assessment to characterise the clone
